## Proof

Let $f(z)$ be single-valued and meromorphic inside the closed contour $C$, with exactly one pole at $z_0 \in \operatorname{int}(C)$. Let $g(z) = f'(z)$ be its derivative.

**Key observation.** Since $f$ is single-valued, for any small positively-oriented circle $\gamma$ around $z_0$ (lying in a punctured neighborhood where $f$ is holomorphic),

$$\oint_\gamma g(z)\,dz = \oint_\gamma f'(z)\,dz = f(z)\big|_{\text{closed loop}} = 0,$$

because $f$ returns to its starting value after one traversal of $\gamma$ (single-valuedness). Hence the residue of $g = f'$ at $z_0$ is

$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0} f'(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma f'(z)\,dz = 0.$$

**Equivalently, via Laurent series.** Write near $z_0$:
$$f(z) = \sum_{n=-m}^{\infty} a_n (z-z_0)^n.$$
Then
$$f'(z) = \sum_{n=-m}^{\infty} n\,a_n (z-z_0)^{n-1} = \sum_{k=-m-1}^{\infty} (k+1)a_{k+1}(z-z_0)^k.$$
The coefficient of $(z-z_0)^{-1}$ (i.e. $k=-1$) is $(-1+1)a_0 = 0$. So $\operatorname{Res}_{z_0} f' = 0$.

**Applying the residue theorem.** The only singularity of $g$ inside $C$ is the pole at $z_0$ (the same pole as $f$, of order $m+1$). By the residue theorem,

$$\int_C g(z)\,dz = 2\pi i \sum \operatorname{Res}(g) = 2\pi i \cdot \operatorname{Res}_{z=z_0} f'(z) = 2\pi i \cdot 0 = 0.$$

**Conclusion.** Even though $g$ has a pole inside $C$, that pole carries **zero residue** (being the derivative of a single-valued function). Therefore

$$\boxed{\int_C dz\, g(z) = 0.}$$

The integral is **zero**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
